description_short: Bhante Bodhidhamma explains right awareness (sammā sati) through the Buddha's life story, distinguishing vipassanā meditation from mindfulness in daily life.
description_long:
In this foundational talk, Bhante Bodhidhamma illuminates the meaning of right awareness (sammā sati) by tracing the Buddha's spiritual journey from existential crisis to awakening. He describes how the young Siddhattha Gotama, despite mastering the jhānas under accomplished teachers and nearly killing himself through extreme asceticism, still found no lasting solution to the fundamental unsatisfactoriness of existence. The turning point came with a childhood memory—watching his father's ploughing ceremony with the open, curious awareness of a child, free from conceptual overlay.

This pivotal insight reveals the essence of vipassanā practice: returning to what Zen calls 'original mind'—the direct, non-conceptual awareness we possessed before language and concepts filtered our experience. Bhante explains that every meditation technique ultimately aims to separate our intuitive intelligence from its entanglement with the intellect and accumulated mental habits. The three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa)—impermanence, the role of desire in suffering, and not-self—inform our looking without becoming objects of thought during practice.

Bhante carefully distinguishes between vipassanā meditation, where we establish an 'observation post' of pure receptivity, and mindfulness in daily life, which requires clear comprehension (sampajañña) while engaged in action. In daily life, we maintain awareness of both outer activity and inner states—knowing when irritation or boredom arises without identifying with it—allowing wise intention to guide our responses. The talk concludes with practical guidance on using sense experiences throughout the day to cultivate this direct, childlike awareness.
